title: The World Cup Starts on Thursday. The Chaos Started Months Ago.
excerpt: Ticket price manipulation, visa denials, a referee turned away at the airport, and mass protests planned for the opener — the 2026 FIFA World Cup in North America is already the most controversial in history. For NRIs, the mess is in their backyard.
body:
When FIFA awarded the 2026 World Cup to the United States, Canada, and Mexico in 2018, the promise was simple: the biggest tournament in history, held across the biggest stadiums in the world, in three countries with the infrastructure to deliver it seamlessly.

With the opening match between Mexico and South Africa at the Azteca Stadium in Mexico City now two days away, "seamless" is not the word anyone is using. "Chaos" is.

The controversies have stacked up so fast that each new scandal barely has time to breathe before the next one arrives.

**The Ticket Scandal**

Start with ticket prices. Between October 2025 and April 2026, FIFA quietly raised prices on more than 90 of the tournament's 104 matches. The average increase across the three core ticket categories was 34 percent. Group-stage tickets that were originally priced under $400 climbed past $600. Premium face-value seats for the final in East Rutherford, New Jersey, touched $10,990.

On the secondary market, it got worse. Individual tickets for the championship match have been listed for as much as $2 million on approved resale platforms.

The attorneys general of New York, New Jersey, and California have all launched investigations. New Jersey AG Jennifer Davenport described FIFA's ticketing system as "a gauntlet of confusion, fake scarcity, and impossibly high prices — all at the expense of consumers." FIFA has been subpoenaed for transaction and marketing data for matches at MetLife Stadium, SoFi Stadium, and Levi's Stadium.

For Indian-American families in the Bay Area, Los Angeles, and the New York metro — where group-stage matches will be played at stadiums a short drive from home — the pricing has turned what should have been a once-in-a-generation live experience into a calculation about whether a family of four can justify spending several thousand dollars for ninety minutes of football.

**The Iran Visa Crisis**

The geopolitical storm has been even more damaging to FIFA's credibility. Iran's national football team spent weeks uncertain whether they would even be allowed into the United States to play their Group G matches.

After the U.S. and Israel launched air strikes on Iran in late February, the Iranian squad moved its planned base camp from Arizona to Tijuana, Mexico. Visa negotiations dragged on until last Friday — just ten days before Iran's first match against New Zealand in Los Angeles on June 15.

The players eventually received visas. Several staff members did not — including the team manager, two analysts, the media director, and a Foreign Ministry representative. The U.S. has said some officials, including Iranian football chief Mehdi Taj, have links to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The Department of Homeland Security clarified on Tuesday that Iranian players will be permitted to enter the U.S. the day before each match, contradicting earlier reports that they would have to arrive and leave on match day. "Thanks to the generosity of President Trump," a DHS spokesperson said, "the Iranian team will be able to arrive the day before their matches."

And then came the tickets. Iran's football federation announced Tuesday that its official allocation of fan tickets had been revoked without explanation — leaving thousands of Iranian supporters who had already booked flights and hotels with no guaranteed way to attend.

**The Referee Who Was Not Allowed In**

Somali referee Omar Artan, selected by FIFA to officiate at the World Cup, was denied entry at Miami airport. U.S. Customs and Border Protection said he "was determined to be inadmissible due to vetting concerns." A World Cup referee, vetted and approved by FIFA's own refereeing committee, turned away at the gate.

**The Protests**

In Mexico City, multiple protest groups have announced plans for mass demonstrations on the morning of the opening match on Thursday. Campaign organizers say they intend to target arterial roads to the Azteca. Some observers believe that if the protests succeed, the kickoff could be delayed — an unprecedented embarrassment for FIFA on the world's biggest stage.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who has not held a press conference in three years, is scheduled to address the media at the Azteca on Wednesday. He will face questions about ticket manipulation, the immigration crisis, the Trump peace prize that he created, and whether the tournament he spent years building is already coming apart.

**What NRIs Need to Know**

For the estimated four million Indian Americans living within driving distance of a World Cup venue — in Los Angeles, the Bay Area, Houston, Dallas, New York, and Miami — the practical advice is straightforward but sobering:

Tickets on the secondary market are real but expensive. Expect to pay $300-$800 for group-stage seats. The final is essentially inaccessible unless money is not a constraint.

Zee Entertainment's Unite8 Sports channels and Zee5 will broadcast all matches in India and across the South Asian subcontinent. For NRIs in North America, Fox, FS1, Telemundo, and Peacock will carry every game.

The tournament runs from June 11 to July 19. The U.S. opens against Paraguay in Los Angeles on June 12. Despite the chaos surrounding the buildup, the football itself — 48 teams, 104 matches, 16 host cities across three countries — remains the most ambitious World Cup ever staged.

Whether the off-field controversies overshadow the on-field spectacle is a question that Thursday's opening ceremony at the Azteca will begin to answer.
